outline.topic: The Wallis Product: Unlocking Pi Through Infinite Fractions
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a background in basic calculus.

sections.title: Introduction: The Geometry-Algebra Bridge
sections.content: Begin with the classic geometric definition of Pi (circumference/diameter) using a circle. Introduce the surprising idea that Pi can also be expressed as an infinite product of simple rational numbers. Use an animation of a circle unfolding into a straight number line to hook the audience.
sections.example: An animated 'Pi-Bot' character uses a compass to draw a circle, then pulls the circle's edge to reveal an infinite string of fractions: (2/1 * 2/3 * 4/3 * 4/5...).

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Powers of Sine
sections.content: Introduce the integral of sin^n(x) from 0 to π/2, denoted as I_n. Visualize the area under the curve for n=1, 2, 3, and 4. Show how the area 'shrinks' and changes shape as the exponent increases. This sets the stage for the reduction formula.
sections.example: A series of overlapping shaded graphs where sin(x) is a tall hill and sin^10(x) is a thin needle, highlighting that the area decreases as 'n' grows.

sections.title: The Recursive Pattern: The Reduction Formula
sections.content: Present the integration by parts result: I_n = ((n-1)/n) * I_{n-2}. Explain that this allows us to calculate high powers by 'stepping down' two steps at a time. Distinguish between the 'Even path' (ending at I_0 = π/2) and the 'Odd path' (ending at I_1 = 1).
sections.example: A 'calculus ladder' where a character jumps down two rungs at a time. Even-numbered rungs lead to a 'Pi' treasure chest, while odd-numbered rungs lead to a '1' treasure chest.

sections.title: The Ratio and the Sandwich Theorem
sections.content: Explain that since the functions are nested (sin^{n+1} < sin^n < sin^{n-1}), their integrals must follow the same order. Show that the ratio I_n / I_{n-1} approaches 1 as n goes to infinity. This is the 'Squeeze' that forces the even and odd paths to meet.
sections.example: Two walls (Even and Odd formulas) slowly closing in on a central value, represented by an arrow pointing toward 1 on a scale.

sections.title: The Grand Reveal: Wallis's Formula
sections.content: Combine the even and odd paths into a single ratio. Rearrange the terms to isolate π/2 on one side. Show the beautiful symmetry of the final product: (2/1 * 2/3) * (4/3 * 4/5) * (6/5 * 6/7)... and explain its significance in convergence speed.
sections.example: A mechanical 'Fraction Factory' where pairs of integers are bolted together to form the product, eventually displaying the value 1.5707... (π/2) on a digital screen.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Geometry-Algebra Bridge
lecture_lines: Pi relates a circle's circumference to its diameter.
It is usually viewed as a geometric constant.
Surprisingly, Pi also equals an infinite rational product.
John Wallis found this stunning link through calculus.
Let's derive this elegant product from sine integrals.
animations: A white (#FFFFFF) circle appears in center-stage. A yellow (#FFFF00) radius is drawn, and the label $\pi = \frac{C}{d}$ fades in above.
The circle's circumference unrolls from the top, straightening into a horizontal white (#FFFFFF) line segment of length $\pi$.
The Wallis Product formula $\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{2}{1} \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \dots$ fades in below the line segment in light blue (#ADD8E6).
The first three pairs of fractions in the product flash in yellow (#FFFF00) to emphasize the simple rational structure.
The number line segment and the formula align horizontally, with a vertical dashed line connecting the value $\pi/2$ on the line to the formula.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Powers of Sine
lecture_lines: Let I sub n be the integral of sine powers.
Increasing the exponent n shrinks the area under sine.
We examine this area from zero to Pi halves.
animations: Display the integral $I_n = \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n(x) dx$ in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Plot $\sin^1(x)$ (blue, #0000FF) and $\sin^{10}(x)$ (green, #00FF00) curves; shade the area reduction from 0 to $\pi/2$.
Show the inequality $I_n < I_{n-1}$ in yellow (#FFFF00) next to the plots.

storyboard.title: The Recursive Pattern: The Reduction Formula
lecture_lines: Integration by parts gives us a recursive reduction formula.
We compute I sub n by stepping down two units.
Even paths start at Pi halves and descend regularly.
Odd paths begin at one and follow the pattern.
These two branches will soon merge into one formula.
animations: The reduction formula $I_n = \frac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2}$ is displayed in white (#FFFFFF) with a box around it.
Two columns appear: 'Even Path' on the left in gold (#FFD700) and 'Odd Path' on the right in spring green (#00FA9A).
Under 'Even', the sequence $I_4 \to I_2 \to I_0$ is shown. Under 'Odd', $I_5 \to I_3 \to I_1$ is shown.
The final values $I_0 = \pi/2$ and $I_1 = 1$ appear at the bottom of their respective columns in bright white (#FFFFFF).
Highlight the 'step down by 2' pattern in the indices with a pulsing red (#FF0000) bracket.

storyboard.title: The Ratio and the Sandwich Theorem
lecture_lines: Higher powers of sine always produce smaller integral areas.
The ratio of consecutive integrals approaches one at infinity.
This squeeze theorem forces the two paths to meet.
animations: Show the inequality $I_{n+1} < I_n < I_{n-1}$ in white (#FFFFFF).
Transform it into the ratio $\frac{I_{n+1}}{I_{n-1}} < \frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}} < 1$ in light blue (#ADD8E6) by dividing through.

Animate the limit where the ratio $\frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}$ is squeezed to 1 as n grows, with the bounds merging, accompanied by a sandwich icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/sandwich.svg] to represent the Squeeze Theorem.

storyboard.title: The Grand Reveal: Wallis's Formula
lecture_lines: Combining the even and odd sequences reveals a ratio.
As n grows, this ratio equals one exactly.
Rearranging the terms isolates Pi halves on one side.
The result is Wallis's famous infinite string of fractions.
Geometry and algebra unite in this simple, infinite beauty.
animations: The expression for the ratio $\frac{I_{2n}}{I_{2n+1}}$ is built using the even and odd products in white (#FFFFFF).
The formula is rearranged to isolate $\pi/2$ on the left, with all other fractions moving to the right.
The fractions on the right regroup into pairs $(2/1 * 2/3) * (4/3 * 4/5) \dots$ in light blue (#ADD8E6).
The symbol $\approx 1.5707 \dots$ appears in yellow (#FFFF00) next to the product as more terms are added.
The final formula $\frac{\pi}{2} = \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4n^2}{4n^2-1}$ appears in a glowing white (#FFFFFF) box.
